10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates recording a dataset snapshot and linking it to a trained model, already covered in this topic.

code.content:
import hashlib

def snapshot_dataset(data, timestamp):
    # already covered as snapshotting dataset versions in this topic
    content = str(sorted(data)).encode()
    version_id = hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest()[:8]
    return {"version_id": version_id, "timestamp": timestamp, "row_count": len(data)}

dataset_v1 = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
snapshot_v1 = snapshot_dataset(dataset_v1, timestamp="2026-01-01")
print(f"Dataset snapshot v1 (already covered in this topic): {snapshot_v1}")

dataset_v2 = dataset_v1 + [5.0, 6.0]  # already covered as datasets changing over time in this topic
snapshot_v2 = snapshot_dataset(dataset_v2, timestamp="2026-02-01")
print(f"Dataset snapshot v2: {snapshot_v2}")

# already covered as linking data versions to model versions in this topic
trained_model_record = {"model_name": "classifier_v3", "data_version_id": snapshot_v2["version_id"]}
print(f"\nTrained model record (already covered in this topic): {trained_model_record}")
print("This record genuinely lets anyone trace this exact model back to the exact dataset snapshot that trained it")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Data versioning tracks exactly which dataset version trained which model.
It complements model versioning, already covered in Serving, with the other half of the traceability story.
Real datasets grow, get corrected, or get cleaned up, so the same name can mean different content over time.
Data versioning captures a fixed snapshot with its own stable, permanent identifier.
Each trained model records exactly which dataset version it was trained on.
This linkage makes retraining the same model reproducible, avoiding difficult or impossible reproduction.
Tools often store only differences between versions rather than full copies, saving storage.
Comparing data versions helps pinpoint exactly what caused unexpected changes in model behavior.
